claims.text: PGM catalysts achieve high ethanol-oxidation activity because their nanoscale configuration promotes dynamic, localized oxidation-state changes.
Localized oxidation-state changes create a mixed-valence surface layer.
The mixed-valence surface layer enhances the binding and activation of ethanol intermediates.
The mixed-valence surface layer facilitates rapid regeneration of active sites.
Rapid active-site regeneration promotes complete ethanol oxidation and mitigates catalyst poisoning.
The as-synthesized PGM nanoparticles have a relatively uniform oxidation-state distribution.
Controlled potential cycling will shift the catalyst surface toward a mixed-valence oxidation-state distribution relative to constant-potential operation.
Potential cycling produces alternating or patchy oxidized and reduced platinum surface regions.
Adjacent catalyst sites alternate between oxidized and reduced states during reaction cycling.
Sites in one oxidation state favor adsorption of ethanol and its intermediates, while neighboring sites in a complementary oxidation state favor their subsequent oxidation.
Complementary oxidized and reduced sites favor the complete 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Dynamic oxidation-state cycling prevents accumulation of poisoning species that deactivate the catalyst.
Potential-cycled catalysts will exhibit a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than constant-potential controls.
Potential-cycled catalysts will exhibit higher current density than constant-potential controls.
Potential cycling will increase selectivity toward complete oxidation products such as CO2 relative to partial oxidation products.
Potential cycling will improve durability through more rapid regeneration of active sites.
The proposed benefit should occur at moderate ethanol concentrations and applied potentials where mixed-valence-layer formation is kinetically accessible.
The benefit may diminish at extremely high potentials or ethanol concentrations because of rapid poisoning or irreversible surface changes.

The experiment compares a constant-potential control with an otherwise comparable potential-cycled catalyst while monitoring oxidation state, electrochemical activity, product selectivity, and durability.
Failure to detect a dynamic mixed-valence layer, or statistically indistinguishable catalytic performance relative to the control, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
